title: Boardroom crisis: the 1-minute version
headline: The first six hours, in one minute
subtitle: An attack is under way. Three quick decisions, then the bill, choice by choice.

briefing.text: Take all the time you need... I've got all day. You've got until 14:00.

fallout.text: Ah, the ledger. Let's see what your good ideas cost you...

briefing.turtle_intro: Welcome to the room. It's 08:10 and the board is waiting for you. Three decisions, one minute. Let's begin.

timeline.text: The security tool spots 40 GB leaving a file server for an unknown address. The alert lands in a queue.
**Now.** The board meets in the crisis room. You're in the chair.

known: Files on several servers are encrypted, and the encryption is still spreading.
At 07:40, a large volume of data left the network.
unknown: How they got in, and whether they're still in the network.
Whether customer data was copied, and whose.
briefing.spider_line: Six hours. Plenty of time to make a few mistakes... I'm counting on you.
briefing.note_title: A little note for the board
note: Pay €1.2 million in crypto before 14:00 and you'll get the key. If not, at 14:00 the copy goes online and the key disappears.

playbook.intro: Two cards to get you through the first hours. Tap one to open it.

cards.title: Contain, then think
cards.say: A panicking board works for the attacker. Start with the boring moves, in order, and keep the evidence.

rules.headline: Cut the cable, keep the power.
rules.body: Disconnect the affected machines from the network, without switching them off or wiping them. The evidence is in memory and on disk.

rules.headline: Say only what you can prove.
rules.body: "No data was affected" is a promise. If the facts contradict it, nobody will believe your next message.

cards.sign_off: In a crisis, calm is a list you follow in order.

cards.title: Nobody gets through this alone
cards.say: I've seen my share of crises. The boards that came out of them well were never the cleverest. They'd called the right people early, and they'd told the truth.

rules.headline: Call the experts before any big decision.
rules.body: Legal first, then your insurer, the police and an incident response team. The ransom is no exception: paying guarantees nothing, and the money funds the next attack.

rules.headline: Tell the right people, on time.
rules.body: The clock for telling the regulator starts when you become aware of the incident: 72 hours under GDPR, "as soon as possible" in Switzerland. Your customers need to know what to do before the attacker publishes their data.

cards.sign_off: The teams that hold together on a Friday morning had someone looking after them long before.

cat0.label: Cat's first rule: cut the cable

cat2.label: Cat's second rule: say only what you can prove

turtle0.label: Turtle's first rule: call the experts

turtle1.label: Turtle's second rule: tell the right people

decisions_intro.text: Three decisions. You lock them in, I check them. No going back. Keep an eye on the four dials.

decisions.title: Stop the spread
decisions.text: The encryption is jumping from server to server. Dana is on the line and needs an order, now. What do you tell her?

artifact.name: Dana Keller
artifact.text: It's spreading. Fourteen servers in ten minutes, and next on the list is the backup server. Tell me what to do, Sam.

options.text: Cut the affected machines off from the network, but leave them switched on. Nobody wipes anything.
Switch everything off, wipe it all and rebuild. Start again from zero.
options.why: You wiped the evidence along with the problem. Now nobody can show which door I used or what I took, so you have to assume I took everything... And I still have the key to that door.

options.text: Wait until IT has the full picture, then do everything in one go.
options.why: The board wanted the full picture? I finished it for you. By 09:00 the backup server was locked too, and your best way out went with it.

options.text: Tell everyone to restart their computer: that usually sorts out this kind of problem.
options.why: Restarting cleared the memory, and with it the traces the investigators wanted first. My encryption restarted right along with every machine.

decisions.explain: Isolate now, ask questions later. Network cable out: the spread stops. Power left on: the evidence stays in memory and on disk. That's what the investigators will use to find the way in and work out what was copied.
decisions.spider_ok: Hm. Cable pulled, evidence intact. I had nine servers left on my list... and no way left to reach them.
decisions.best: Cut the affected machines off from the network, leave them switched on, wipe nothing.

decisions.title: The ransom
decisions.text: The note demands €1.2 million in crypto before 14:00. After that, the stolen copy goes online and the key is destroyed. What is the board's position?

artifact.name: Dana Keller
artifact.text: Last night's backup is on the same network. I can't promise you it's clean. And the board needs a position on this note before the press gets hold of it.

options.text: Don't pay for now. Call the police, and let legal and the response team look at the backups and the options first.
Pay now, before the countdown runs out. It's the shortest route to getting the files back.
options.why: Thank you for the money... My key unlocked a third of your files. My copy of your data, I kept, naturally. And now I know this board pays.

options.text: Reply from the CEO's email address and haggle over the price yourselves.
options.why: How brave... You wrote like frightened amateurs, and I'm not one. Every reply told me how much those files meant to you. So every reply put the price up.

options.text: Refuse, and tell nobody outside this room. Fewer people in the know, fewer leaks.
options.why: Silence. My favourite. No police, nobody who's dealt with me before... You isolated yourselves. I didn't even have to.

decisions.explain: Paying should never be a reflex. The money doesn't buy a key that's sure to work, or the deletion of the stolen copy, and it funds the next attack. Call the police, bring in legal and the responders, test what your backups actually restore. Then decide on facts. The countdown isn't one.
decisions.spider_ok: No payment, no panic. I can't stand a patient board.
decisions.best: Don't pay for now: bring in the police, legal and the responders, and test the backups first.

decisions.title: Customers and the regulator
decisions.text: The responders confirm it: about 40 GB were copied, including the names, email addresses and hashed passwords of 120,000 customers. The attacker promises to publish everything at 14:00. What do you do about the regulator and your customers?

artifact.name: Luc Marchand
artifact.text: GDPR gives us 72 hours to notify the authority, counting from when we became aware of the incident. Swiss law says "as soon as possible". And our clock has been running since 07:40, whatever we decide.

options.text: Notify the data protection authority now, and prepare a plain message for customers: what happened, what was taken, what they need to do.
Wait for the investigation to finish, then decide who to tell.
options.why: An investigation takes weeks. The legal deadline is three days. The regulator will want to know why you knew on Friday and only spoke up on Tuesday... And fines are calculated as a percentage.

options.text: Say nothing until the data shows up online.
options.why: At 14:00, I published. Your customers heard it from a stranger on a forum, with no warning and no chance to change their password. By evening, several accounts had fallen.

options.text: Email every customer now: "your data is safe". Investigate afterwards.
options.why: "Your data is safe." Lovely sentence, sent an hour before I proved otherwise. It took you years to earn their trust. One sentence was enough to spend it.

decisions.explain: Speak early, speak plainly, tell the truth. The regulator's clock started when you became aware of the incident, and your customers need to change their passwords and watch out for phishing before the attacker comes after them. And never promise them safety you can't prove.
decisions.spider_ok: You told them yourselves, and straight. That leaves me nothing to blackmail you with.
decisions.best: Notify the regulator in time, and tell customers plainly what happened and what they need to do.

contained.title: Every door I tried was shut. Irritating.
contained.body: Isolated, informed, patient, honest, even kind. I didn't care for it. I'll find myself a house with a quieter board... and fewer second factors.
contained.score: Three out of three. None of these decisions needed a clever tool, only taking them in the right order. One last thing: ask your team whether your VPN has a second lock.

bruised.title: Still standing... but I left you a few marks.
bruised.body: You held on to what mattered. But some of your choices were gifts, and I accepted them. The ledger below tells you which.
bruised.score: Fairly solid. The decisions you got wrong are in the recap, each with the rule that would have prevented it. Read them, then replay.

wrecked.title: What a beautiful disaster. We did good work, you and I.
wrecked.body: In the moment, every one of those choices seemed reasonable. That's why they work so often. So try again, and think about the order this time.
wrecked.score: A hard morning, and it was built to be. Real boards get these same choices wrong. Better to do it here than on a real Friday. Read the recap, then we'll go again.

footer: Until next time... And next time, I won't come in by email. By the way, that second lock on your VPN: have you checked?
